title: The Night the Fridges Warmed Up
objective: Explain how attackers spoiled food across European supermarkets in October and November 2026 without malware or a break-in: they used the internet to force refrigeration controllers into defrost mode. The viewer should leave knowing what happened, why defrost was enough, why old internet-facing controllers were the weak point, and what is still unknown.
audience: General viewers on short-form platforms who follow tech and world news; no knowledge of cybersecurity or refrigeration assumed.

message.core_message: Nobody broke into a single store: attackers told old, internet-exposed refrigeration controllers to defrost, and hundreds of supermarkets across Europe lost their food.
key_points: Wave 1: overnight Sunday 11 to Monday 12 October 2026, France; hundreds of stores across Intermarche, Cooperative U, Carrefour and others, about 700 per the French economy minister
Wave 2: overnight Sunday 1 to Monday 2 November 2026; Belgium, Luxembourg, Sweden, Ireland and others, same pattern
Method: controllers forced into defrost, reportedly stretched to eight hours; cases reached about 50 C, one store 80 C; some equipment caught fire

Why it worked: back-room controllers with web pages on the open internet, many old models that no longer receive security updates; a hidden date-derived daily password had been documented, but its use here is unconfirmed
Food safety: above about 5 C bacteria multiply fast, so affected stock was discarded
A full fix needs a software update and a physical change to the unit (Belgian refrigeration firm)
Nobody has been identified; officials advise taking controllers offline, updating firmware and checking defrost schedules

avoid: hacker-in-hoodie, green-matrix, padlock or skull imagery
red-alert HUD graphics and glitch effects
naming a culprit, a country or a state actor
stating a store count or euro loss as settled fact

constraints: Light canvas throughout; heat is shown by tile colour (ultramarine to marigold to vermilion), not by a dark background
Every number on screen carries its source or 'reported' / 'per' wording where outlets disagree
Attribution is stated as unknown; the Claroty flaw is stated as unconfirmed
Retailer names appear as plain text only; no logos, no store fronts, no real photographs
The picture changes every 2-3 s; narration never plays over a static frame
Portrait only unless more formats are requested (docs/VISION.md default)
Re-check counts and the country list on the day of render; reporting is still moving (see research.md open items)

references.description: Workspace technique records may be consulted at storyboard time (grid-based and counter techniques in catalogue/data/references/). Techniques only; no assets, brands or footage.

audio.notes: Voice am_adam at 1.15. Room tone: a low refrigeration-compressor hum (about 55 Hz plus soft broadband) that CUTS OUT at the moment the first tile warms, which is what a compressor does when defrost starts; after that a sparse, slow tick like a thermostat relay, climbing slowly in pitch with temperature. Dim minimalist pulse bed at about -26 dBFS from scene 2. Tactile micro-sounds on counter rolls and stamps. No whooshes on dissolves.

research.reason: Developing news story with disputed and provisional figures, technical claims about a named vendor's product, and food-safety claims. See research.md.

creative_directions.name: Thermal grid
creative_directions.concept: The whole film is one grid of fridge-door tiles on a cool white sheet, each tile a small mono readout: 4 for chilled, -18 for frozen. Quiet, ordered, ultramarine. One tile ticks up and the colour spreads across the grid like a rumour, ultramarine to marigold to vermilion, until the sheet is hot. The same grid then does all the explaining: one tile opens into a defrost cutaway, a controller tile reaches out to a field of exposed dots, the grid empties as stock is discarded, then dissolves into a dot map of Europe where the second wave lights up. The ending cools the grid back to ultramarine one tile at a time and holds. It delivers the pitched hook (a cyberattack shown through thousands of fridges slowly warming) as a single continuous transformation with no computers in sight.

visual_identity.palette: paper #FBFBFA, paper-2 #F0EFEC, ink #17171A, ink-2 #5B5B63, rule #D9D8D4, cold ultramarine #1D5A8A, warning marigold #E0A100, hot vermilion #C1272D; the ramp ultramarine to marigold to vermilion encodes temperature everywhere in the film and is used for nothing else
visual_identity.typography: Playfair Display for the big temperature numerals and dates, Inter for support lines, JetBrains Mono for tile readouts, timestamps and sources
visual_identity.texture: none; thin rules and subtle paper tints only (per the style)

motion_language.personality: calm and exact at the start, then relentless: the heat moves at constant speed while everything else stays still
signature_moves: grid-wave colour contagion from one tile
counter-roll of degrees on a hero tile
stamp of a dated ledger line
tiles emptying to outline one by one
motion_language.transitions: match cuts that reuse the grid as the continuous element; crossfade only between scenes 5 and 6; no whooshes

composition.approach: Portrait 720x1280: the grid or scene art fills the upper two-thirds inside the safe area; one line of copy and a mono source line sit below it above the bottom UI safe zone. The hero numeral sits in the top third when it counts.

creative_directions.pacing: new picture or beat every 2-3 s; scenes 12-18 s; final hold of 2.5 s
creative_directions.why_it_fits: One simple visual system carries the hook, the mechanism, the scale and the second wave, keeps a light canvas, and puts the heat on screen as the only dramatic element.

creative_directions.name: Supermarket cutaway diorama
creative_directions.concept: A flat cross-section of a store at night: shelves, cases, the back room with a small controller box, the dark street outside. Warmth is shown with heat-haze lines rising from the cases while shoppers' world sleeps.

composition.approach: wide cutaway cropped for portrait with a slow pan

creative_directions.why_it_fits: Friendly and clear, but it shows one store, so the scale (hundreds of stores, several countries) is told rather than shown, and a wide cutaway wastes a portrait frame.

creative_directions.name: Overnight incident log
creative_directions.concept: Led by a single temperature-versus-time line chart from 22:00 to 08:00, with timestamps typed in mono and annotation callouts: defrost starts, alarms silent, staff arrive, bin the stock.

composition.approach: chart fills the portrait frame with callouts stacked below

creative_directions.pacing: chart draws in a few long beats
creative_directions.why_it_fits: Precise and credible, but the time series is illustrative (no reported minute-by-minute data exists), so it risks implying data we do not have, and it has no answer to the pitched 'thousands of fridges' hook.

success_criteria: The first 3 seconds show a grid of cold tiles and the first tile warming; no title card before the hook
The temperature ramp (ultramarine to marigold to vermilion) is used for temperature only
Each reported number appears with its source or a 'reported' qualifier
The unknowns (who, which vendors in wave 2, whether the known flaw was used) are stated aloud, not only on screen
Each scene is readable at phone size with sound off
The ending holds for at least 2 seconds
